articles.title: Hooked on tuna: People have been harvesting these ocean predators for 44,000 years
articles.author:
<name>Emma Elliott Smith, Research Associate in Anthropology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/emma-elliott-smith-2766010"/>
paras: From a humble mayonnaise-laden sandwich to an expensive piece of sashimi, tuna is a prized source of food for people around the world. Once an inexpensive, easily shipped canned protein source, today’s bluefin tunas can fetch millions of dollars at auction . Millions of tons of tuna are harvested every year, supporting a global industry worth around US$40 billion annually .
But tunas are more than just the pink flesh found in cans and sushi, and humanity’s story with these fish goes back further than you might expect.
As a biologist and an archaeologist interested in long-term human-environment interactions, we wanted to investigate the deep record of people’s relationship with tunas.

We drew on the expertise of 18 leading researchers worldwide and studied a variety of sources, from the skeletal remains of tunas in archaeological sites to ancient rock art, paintings on frescos and vases, written historical records and ethnographic accounts from Indigenous communities. This data helped us understand where, when and why people caught tunas, and what cultural and environmental forces shaped these early fisheries. In turn, this provided new insights into how past harvests compare with the millions of tons caught today.
“Tuna” is a common name given to a group of 15 fish species . The major market species include eight “true tunas” in genus Thunnus along with skipjack tuna ( Katsuwonus pelamis ).

Tunas are among the largest predators in the open ocean, with some species reaching almost 10 feet (over 3 meters) in length and living for over 40 years . Tuna are champion swimmers; Pacific bluefin tuna can migrate 5,000 miles (8,000 kilometers) across the northern Pacific in a matter of months .

Tuna are also ecologically important apex predators and serve as sentinels of ocean health . However, most scientific research has focused on the past 75 years, with assessments of the health of tuna populations benchmarked against the year 1950 . The focus on recent decades raises a variety of questions about the deeper history of fishing for tuna prior to the past century.

The oldest definitive evidence of tuna fishing, in the form of skeletal remains of what were likely skipjack tuna, comes from East Timor in southeast Asia about 44,000 years ago . Likely aided by deepwater channels that brought tunas close to shore, this early example of tuna fishing is somewhat unusual – most areas of the world don’t contain evidence of tuna fishing until 10,000 years ago or more recently.

Ancient fishers in Japan and Korea, for instance, captured tunas beginning at least 7,000 years ago, with a rich culinary tradition and large-scale harvests that trace their way to the present day love for these fishes in the region.

The northeastern Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea are home to one of the world’s oldest and most important tuna fisheries, focused on Atlantic bluefin tuna. A few ancient tuna bones found in a Neanderthal site in Gibraltar dating to around 26,000 years ago may have been obtained by Neanderthals scavenging. However, by 9,000 to 11,000 years ago, thousands of tuna bones were deposited in Greece in a cave overlooking Kiladha Bay. The number of sites across Europe with tuna remains increases rapidly in the archaeological record after about 8,000 years ago .

These early fishers used a variety of methods to catch tuna , including hook and line, harpoons, and traps or nets. They often took advantage of topographic features where fish could be driven close to shore. This tuna fishing is captured in written records, paintings and other art, showing the cultural importance of these fish to ancient European societies. The ancient Greeks deemed tuna worthy of sacrifice to the gods and used them as offerings to Poseidon .

By 3,000 years ago, a commercial Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery had formed in the Mediterranean, with large-scale trade and specialized nets and traps. By the 16th and 17th centuries, people may have caught tens of thousands of tons annually . This fishery was made possible by the predictable migration patterns of Atlantic bluefin and coastal access to tunas – no dangerous oceanic voyages necessary.
For over 5,000 years, Indigenous people on North America’s northwest coast, particularly in Nuu-chah-nulth territory, had an important and complex fishery for Pacific bluefin tuna .

Ethnographic accounts from native elders describe how during unique warm-water events in late summer, people voyaged out at night into the fjords, aided by natural bioluminescent plankton. With spotters overlooking the fjords and communicating from land, fishers set fires in canoes to lure tuna close enough to harpoon. People would spear these massive fish, some perhaps more than 6 feet (2 meters) in length and weighing 640 pounds (290 kilograms). Bluefin tuna vertebrae have been found in 23 regional archaeological sites .

In Southern California, people also captured tunas, particularly around Santa Catalina Island, where Indigenous fishers caught Pacific bluefin, yellowfin, albacore and skipjack tunas for 6,000 years, leaving the fishes’ skeletal remains in regional archaeological sites.

However, it wasn’t until the 19th and 20th centuries that commercial and sport fisheries for tuna developed in the area. Tuna experienced a meteoric rise in popularity during World War I and World War II. Often centered around canneries in Los Angeles and San Diego, Southern California commercial and industrial tuna fisheries benefited from Japanese and Portuguese immigrant fishing communities, which helped spawn a global industry for tuna.
Tuna consumption by people is obviously nothing new. But how has the scale of tuna harvest changed through time?

Using the quantity of tuna bones present in archaeological sites as a rough metric, we found that even the largest of these ancient fisheries – those in the Mediterranean – likely only removed thousands of tonnes of tuna over millennia, which pales in comparison to the millions of tons of tuna now removed from the oceans every year.

This contrast brings up important questions: What are the consequences of oceanic exploitation exploding over such a relatively short period of time? How can people sustainably manage tuna populations? There are no easy answers, and three of the commercially important tuna species – southern bluefin, Pacific bluefin and bigeye tuna – remain endangered, vulnerable or near threatened . However, in several regions a combination of effective governance, monitoring and harvest controls have stabilized tuna populations even with intensive harvests.

The deep history of tuna fishing also highlights the human capacity for innovation. For more than 44,000 years, people have found ways to locate, catch and share tunas. That same capacity, channeled into international cooperation and science-based management, may help maintain global tuna stocks at sustainable levels – even if they’ll likely never again reach precommercial fishing levels of abundance.

articles.title: 300 glaciers have disappeared from the American West since the mid-20th century – the survivors have a few things in common
articles.author:
<name>Andrew Fountain, Professor of Geography, Portland State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-fountain-2770507"/>
paras: From an airplane, most of the glaciers of the Rocky Mountain West look like small patches of white nestled into rugged landscape where the topography folds. The white is the snow cover, and lower down you can see the gray-blue bare ice.

In the middle of the 20th century, over 1,450 glaciers could be found in the contiguous U.S. Together, they covered 217 square miles (562 square kilometers) in six western states. Today, a comprehensive review my colleagues and I just published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows their total area has shrunk by 35% and they are still shrinking, perhaps faster.
A little more than 300 glaciers have disappeared , way more than I had anticipated.

Those that survive reflect just how vulnerable mountain glaciers have become as global temperatures rise . Where glaciers once covered large expanses of the western mountains thousands of years ago, most of the remaining glaciers in the Rockies and Sierra Nevada are small and found in topographically protected places.

When people think of glaciers, they often picture huge ice streams with icebergs calving off the front, like you’ll find in Alaska or Greenland. In the Lower 48 states, with the exception of a few large glaciers in Washington, they’re much smaller.

We found that the average glacier area is about one-tenth of a square mile (about a quarter of a square kilometer) in size. The area of the largest glacier, found on Washington’s Mount Rainier, is about 4.3 square miles (11.24 square kilometers).

I was surprised to find that glaciers in the Rocky Mountains – those in Colorado, Montana and Wyoming and in the Sierra Nevada of California – subsist because of their unique position on the landscape, which somewhat insulates them from the otherwise less-favorable regional climate.

The surviving Rocky Mountain glaciers inhabit shaded niches less exposed to direct sunshine and gain additional snow from avalanches. If these glaciers were exposed to more sun and less snow accumulation, they likely wouldn’t exit at all.
We found the fastest-thinning glaciers are in the Beartooth-Absaroka Mountains of the Rockies in southern Montana, which are losing about 1.5 feet (about half a meter) of ice thickness per year.

It’s a different story in Washington, where the glaciers on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker are much larger, have cooler summers and get a lot more snowfall. Although they too are shrinking, they do so at a much slower rate, about half a foot of ice thickness per year. The glacier area on Mount Rainier alone is greater than the total sum in all the other states.

In Washington, generally speaking, the higher you go, the less glacier loss you find. That makes sense; it’s cooler at higher elevations. But in the Rocky Mountain region there is no similar trend, suggesting the survivors are niche glaciers that depend on local topographic benefits.

In a study a few years ago, colleagues and I modeled the glaciers on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula and found most would disappear by 2070 under current climate trends. That indicates that glaciers elsewhere are probably not far behind.

The Olympics are vulnerable because they’re close to the Pacific Ocean at somewhat lower elevation. The other Washington glaciers, particularly on Mount Rainier and Mount Baker, will likely survive past 2100, but how much longer is an open question.

The principal importance of the glaciers is to provide water to high alpine ecosystems . The glaciers partially melt in late summer, providing cool water for cold-adapted fish and other stream life. They provide a water supply that’s otherwise absent in the dry late summer, after the seasonal snow disappears, when the region doesn’t get a lot of rain.
While the glaciers of the Rockies are primarily important for ecosystems at this point, those in Washington also contribute to hydropower production .

An important hazard is also associated with the glaciers on the steep-sided volcanoes of the Cascade Range, which stretches from California to Washington. The moraines formed by these glaciers are large, partly due to the highly erodible volcanic rock beneath the ice. Moving ice deposits eroded rocks, forming aprons at their lower ends. As the glaciers retreat, they leave the accumulated rocks behind as steep-sided moraines that are no longer buttressed by the ice.

High water flows from rain or glacier melt can undercut the moraines, triggering landslides and creating debris flows that go rocketing down the mountains. This happened in 2006 on Mount Hood and Mount Rainier and closed a number of highways. We’ll see that happen more often as the glaciers retreat.
The shrinking and eventual loss of all of these glaciers will affect ecosystems across the West, as well as waterways humans and wildlife rely on.
Andrew Fountain receives funding from the US Forest Service.

articles.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
articles.author:
<name>William Blomquist, Professor Emeritus of Political Science, Indiana University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/william-blomquist-2689440"/>
paras: In 1638, John Harvard , an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death.

In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets .

Based on our decades of experience as scholars , academic administrators and school fundraisers , we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times.

Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts , student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States .

University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package . The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments . A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria.
There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate .
Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever , students and their families are still struggling to pay for college .

Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone , including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont.
And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College , which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network.
Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before.
The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025.

Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research .
On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities.

It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University . And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million .

The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes . The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities , those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades . In 2024 it slipped below 7% . Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025 . Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts.

In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts.
Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference.

In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns.

Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors.
2. Donating with few or no strings attached
Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs.
Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change.

Brandeis University , Indiana University , Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic.

Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies , such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts.

In 1920, the trustees of Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky, passed a resolution placing future unrestricted bequests, donations made through people’s estates, in the school’s endowment. Berea students do not pay for tuition, fees, housing or food – thanks in large part to those unrestricted donations.
3. Helping students afford all college costs so they can graduate
Supporting students directly helps them go to college, stay in school and graduate .

Donors already make gifts that fund schools’ financial aid packages, with about $7 billion in gifts designated for this purpose in 2025 . But the colleges and universities that receive the most dollars from donors serve a small fraction of the nation’s undergraduate students – and not those from low-income families . We recommend that donors consider making gifts to the thousands of colleges and universities, including community colleges, that don’t typically draw big donations and have endowments totaling in the millions, rather than billions, of dollars .

Sometimes it takes more than tuition scholarships for students to graduate. Donors can pay for additional expenses, such as transportation and textbooks, and fund extra academic advising and mentoring. Billionaire philanthropists John and Laura Arnold’s Commit2Completion grant program at Arizona’s Maricopa Community Colleges addresses those kinds of often overlooked priorities.

You don’t have to be very wealthy to fund scholarships. Anyone can pitch in through platforms like Dollars for Scholars . This program’s more than 400 chapters enable local donors to pool their gifts to help students raised in their communities pay college expenses. For example, a rural Minnesota chapter awarded $248,000 to 65 college-bound students in 2025.

There are also hundreds of other place-based “ promise programs ” that provide tuition and fees scholarships to public colleges and universities in their areas and offer programming such as college readiness workshops and access to local employers.

Philanthropy can’t solve every problem higher education faces. But by giving together, donating with fewer strings attached and helping students pay their college expenses, alumni and other donors can be strategic in how they help.

articles.title: Pardoning of Israeli soldier evokes a long history of clemency for those who kill Palestinians
articles.author:
<name>Tamir Sorek, Liberal Arts Professor of Middle East History, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tamir-sorek-411715"/>
paras: The pardoning of Elor Azaria , a former Israeli soldier convicted of killing a wounded Palestinian man in the occupied West Bank, comes with a history.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision itself – announced on Sept. 19, 2026 – came more than eight years after Azaria left prison .
The immediate effect is that it clears Azaria of his criminal record. But its public significance is broader – and reaches much further back.

I study how Israelis have talked about Palestinian lives and deaths over the past century. In my forthcoming book , I trace a recurring idea: Palestinians are viewed as an obstacle to Israel’s territorial and security goals, and whose removal can be imagined as necessary or justified . Azaria’s pardon fits into this notion, showing how the state’s response to killing Palestinians can be expressed through the language of mercy for the perpetrator – and it is a pattern that goes back almost 80 years.

The details of Azaria’s case are fairly straightforward. On March 24, 2016, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif and another Palestinian armed with knives attacked an Israeli soldier in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Al-Sharif was shot and lay wounded on the ground. Minutes later, Azaria approached and shot him in the head.
Video of the killing circulated widely . An Israeli military court convicted Azaria of manslaughter in 2017 and sentenced him to 18 months in prison. He was released after serving nine months.
Justifying his decision, Herzog’s office cited the years that had passed , Azaria’s expression of sorrow in his application for a pardon, and the approach of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.
Yet Azaria had said after his release that he would act the same way again . While the conviction will remain part of the historical record, the pardon removes any lasting consequence for him.
Herzog’s decision was warmly received by some in Israel, where Azaria’s case had been taken up by the political right .

For human rights watchers, it is a worrying development. “The president’s decision is a clear demonstration that the Israeli justice system is neither willing nor able to enforce the law against soldiers who harm Palestinians,” noted Ziv Stahl , director of the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.
However unequal that may appear to critics now, it is a trend with precedents reaching back to Israel’s founding.

During the Arab-Israeli war between 1947 and 1949, some 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes . It was an expulsion that could not have happened without extreme violence, including dozens of massacres by Zionist militias and Israeli army.
The perpetrators were rarely, if ever, punished.

In November 1948, though, Israeli soldiers killed civilians in Hula , a village in Lebanon. This time, the direct commander of the operation arrested the officer who ordered the massacre and complained about him. An Israeli military court convicted company commander Shmuel Lahis of murdering 15 people and sentenced him to seven years in prison.
On appeal, his sentence was reduced to one year. Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, then canceled his prison sentence in 1950 .

Five years later, President Yitzhak Ben-Zvi pardoned Lahis. Decades later, in 1978, Lahis was appointed director general of the Jewish Agency , the primary Zionist organization promoting Jewish immigration and settlement in Israel.
These were distinct decisions, but together they show how a conviction for murdering Arab civilians eventually lost its practical and lasting consequences.

The Lahis case nevertheless established an early precedent for leniency toward an Israeli soldier convicted of murdering Arab civilians. It continued in the years that followed, when Israel, for several years after its independence, pursued an unofficial policy of shooting Palestinian refugees who attempted to return to their homes, their land, or the property they had left behind. Costing the lives of thousands until the mid-1950s , this unofficial open-fire policy turned the new border into a lethal instrument for making the results of the expulsion permanent.
That precedent became clearer after the massacre at Kafr Qasim.

On Oct. 29, 1956, Israeli Border Police killed Palestinian citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village 12 miles (19 km) from Tel Aviv. Authorities had moved the start of a curfew forward without ensuring that villagers working outside knew about it. In all, Israeli troops killed 47 people. In the trial that followed, eight troops were convicted of murder and sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven to 17 years.
The ensuing military trial produced a principle taught for decades later in Israel: Soldiers must refuse an order that is manifestly illegal .

What happened after the convictions is less often remembered. The prison terms were reduced on appeal and, for some, reduced again by the military chief of staff. In November 1959, President Ben-Zvi shortened the sentences of the last two men still in prison, Shmuel Malinki and Gavriel Dahan. Both were released by March 1960. Less than 18 months after sentencing, every person convicted in the main trial was free.
Kafr Qasim, thus, left two legacies: The court drew a boundary against unlawful killing while other state authorities sharply limited the consequences for crossing it.

The pattern did not end with those early cases. Since the first Palestinian intifada , or uprising, began in 1987, human rights organizations have documented how seldom investigations into Israeli soldiers’ killings of Palestinians resulted in prosecution .

From the beginning of the second intifada in 2000 through March 2011, Israeli forces in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip killed at least 3,024 Palestinians who were not taking part in combat, according to the Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem. Of all such incidents, only 12 soldiers were indicted, and not a single one was convicted of murder .

My research points to the same pattern across a longer period. Throughout Israel’s history, even in the rare cases of conviction of a soldier or a policeman for killing Palestinians, the maximum time a perpetrator spent in prison was three years and four months.

This measures time served, rather than the sentences initially announced by courts – a distinction made especially clear by Kafr Qasim and reinforced by the Azaria case today. After all, the former military medic served just nine months of an 18-month sentence for the killing of a wounded Palestinian. And even then, was deemed to be suitable for a pardon.

In so doing, Herzog is nodding to the past, but also signaling to soldiers on the ground today that killing a Palestinian is forgivable. The pardon transforms what is sometimes presented as an aberration into part of the state’s moral order

articles.title: More than 119 million Brazilians voted in the Oct. 4 election – including about 21,000 Florida residents
articles.author:
<name>Rafael R. Ioris, Professor of Modern Latin America History, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rafael-r-ioris-1379877"/>
paras: More than 119 million Brazilians voted on Oct. 4, 2026, in the national elections to select the country’s next president and the governors of all 27 states, among other government officials.
That’s nearly 75% of the approximately 159 million eligible voters. Unlike in the U.S., voting is mandatory in Brazil for all citizens between the ages of 18 and 70 .
This includes nearly 1 million Brazilians who currently live outside the country . About 265,000 Brazilians call the U.S. home, with small but growing communities in Boston, New York and Miami .

Because neither incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nor his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro , managed to get over 50% of the votes , Brazilians at home and abroad will have to turn out again on Oct. 25 for a runoff election.

Brazil does not have a long tradition of democracy. But it does have a secure and sophisticated election system. As a scholar of Latin American history and politics , and a Brazilian citizen living in the U.S., I watched these elections with great interest.

Brazilians living abroad are required by law to vote, but they may not cast ballots by mail or online. In many countries, Brazilian consulates serve as the polling places for the diaspora population. Because the U.S. is so spread out, the Brazilian government sets up 15 polling places in 12 states . Two of these are in Florida – one in the Orlando area, where about 26,000 Brazilian voters live, and one in Miami, which is home to the third-largest concentration of Brazilians in the U.S., with more than 40,000 registered voters.

Voting takes place in a single day – always a Sunday – through electronic voting machines, and results are known within a few hours. Though it is compulsory, the penalty for not voting is just a small fine – about US$1 – and as long as a citizen notifies the government within two months of the election that they did not vote, they remain in good legal standing.
So it’s not surprising that only about 75,000 Brazilians – roughly 28% of eligible voters – cast their ballots in the U.S. on Oct. 4.

It’s unclear whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations prevented people from voting, though some Brazilians say they believe fear of ICE contributed to a lower turnout than in 2022, when more than 37% of eligible voters cast their ballots. Organizations for expats in the U.S. warned Brazilians that if their immigration status was precarious , they should not vote.

What is clear is the importance of this election for the future of Latin America’s largest economy and society, as well as for the future of Brazil-U.S. relations. If reelected, Lula is likely to continue to resist overt pressures from Washington to weaken Brazil’s economic ties with China.

On the other hand, Flávio Bolsonaro has signaled that he plans to have much closer relations with the U.S . That is why President Donald Trump would prefer to have a Bolsonaro in power, so that the U.S. influence in Latin America may be further consolidated.

Among Brazilian voters who were abroad on Election Day, Lula won in 64 out of 101 countries where voting was made available by Brazilian diplomatic authorities. But Flávio Bolsonaro won in some of the nations with the largest numbers of Brazilian residents . This includes the U.S., Japan and neighboring countries in South America.

In the U.S., Brazilian voters cast 45,004 ballots for Flávio Bolsonaro and 23,335 for Lula. This seems to be another indication of the polarization that has shaped this key election and, more broadly, the general political context of Brazil in the past few years.
I was not surprised to see that Flávio Bolsonaro finished in the lead on Oct. 4, as the electoral pendulum across the region has been swinging to the right of the political spectrum for some time.

Even though Lula managed to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, Bolsonarismo – the extreme-right political movement that carries his name – has remained the most influential political force in the country . This is a right-wing movement whose leaders, especially members of the Bolsonaro family, have openly and consistently called for the revival of Brazil’s military regime that ruled the country from the mid-1960s to mid-1980s.

Now that Flávio Bolsonaro, an otherwise irrelevant senator from the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the staunch political base of the Bolsonaros is located, has finished ahead of Lula in the first round of elections , it seems clear that the extreme right has the upper hand in Brazil today.
A few years ago, Brazil seemed on track to becoming a mature democracy , after having held several electoral cycles with peaceful transfers of power to opposition candidates.
But now, considering the lack of commitment to democratic traditions in the Bolsonarismo movement , this trend risks being derailed, ironically, by means of a democratic election.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: Where I agree with AI ‘doomer’ Max Tegmark, and where I think he’s wrong
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: Regular readers of this column may have wondered about the long gap since my Sept. 4 column, “ What kids tell chatbots, but not you .” Well, it’s hard to write business-as-usual AI columns during the great AI freakout . I’ve realized that I won’t be able to do justice to this topic in one column, and that life goes on. As the economist Antoine Levy pointed out , OpenAI employees warn that we may all die within a few years yet still fund their 401(k) accounts.

I’m easing into the topic of AI risks by sharing a recent debate I had with Max Tegmark , an MIT professor and a leading AI doomer. The New York Post set this up as optimist against doomer, but I consider myself an AI realist.

Tegmark noted that Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon have converged on AI, and took it as good news. It terrified me. AI needs rules written by people who understand it, not by demagogues. Tegmark said that AI is less regulated than a sandwich shop, but we have plenty of sandwich shops and zero superintelligence (so far). I believe that we should address what exists: the hackers who already use AI to break into companies for the price of lunch.

A condensed version of the debate follows. Words in quotation marks are verbatim, and the rest is paraphrased. You can view the debate on YouTube . Several exchanges refer to this summer’s incident , in which OpenAI test agents got out of their sandbox and hacked Hugging Face.

Tegmark: Loss of control used to be a forecast, and “now suddenly it’s in the past.” This summer “1,200 rogue bots broke out of this American company,” and “humans didn’t even find out until weeks later.”

Etzioni: The agents weren’t rogue . The people “setting the configurations of their sandbox” at OpenAI “failed to put the boundaries on them appropriately.” People made that mistake, and people can fix it.

Etzioni: Cyberattacks and attempts to make bioweapons are “a clear and present danger.” Extinction-level risks are different: “We haven’t seen those yet. We hypothesize, and usually pretty vaguely, on how these will come about.”
Tegmark: The risks Etzioni wants to separate are “connected in their cause.” “If there were some safety standards like there are for other industries, so many of these problems would go away.”
3. Government regulations vs. technical fixes

Tegmark: Do what the auto and pharma industries do, and “have some binding safety standards that the government requires before people can make money off of products.” Companies would have to show that their AI won’t harm kids and won’t slip out of their control. If they can’t show that terrorists won’t use it to make bioweapons, “well, come back when you can, buddy.”

Etzioni: Regulation is necessary, but it has its own risks. “The road to regulatory hell is paved with the EU’s good intentions.” And “we should not underestimate the power of technical solutions.” The author Dan Wang says China is run by engineers and America is run by lawyers, so we naturally talk about regulation and they naturally talk about technical fixes. For bioweapons, the fix may lie “in the transitions from what’s called bits to atoms,” where we can block the physical materials an attacker needs.
Tegmark: “We don’t have to trust China.” The Chinese Communist Party wants to stay in control, so “they will not want to let a Chinese company build uncontrollable superintelligence.”
Etzioni: I don’t trust China. “Nothing would make them happier than us hamstringing ourselves.”

Tegmark: “There’s been more political change in a good direction in the last few months than in the past decade.” It’s like a ketchup bottle: “nothing, nothing, nothing, and then all of it at once.” At my convention I introduced Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon back to back, “which had not been in my bingo card.”
Etzioni: “Can you imagine two worse demagogues?” And “we need to have good solutions, not popular ones.”

Etzioni: “I foresee over time something quite negative happening, and to me the question is whether it’s Hiroshima or the Cuban Missile Crisis.” The Cuban Missile Crisis was a threat averted. Hiroshima was a catastrophe that came before the better rules did.

Tegmark: Self-interest is the fix. Make safety the way companies get rich, and “we’re going to see all the creativity and entrepreneurship of private industry racing to the top to do this instead of racing to the bottom.”
Etzioni: The AI CEOs are self-interested. “When you are on the path to a trillion-dollar-plus IPO, that exerts a gravitational force on your mind.”

Tegmark: “I completely agree with Oren that we need to take what the AI CEOs say with a grain of salt.” Listen to AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio instead: “I don’t think we can dismiss them as just doing it for some money reasons.” The whistleblowers gave up stock options potentially worth $1 million or more to speak out.

Etzioni: I was an AI optimist and I’m now an AI realist. The things I thought were many years away “are either right here, right now, or coming soon at a pace that we may not be able to anticipate.” I’ve learned from Tegmark, and “I was wrong.”
Tegmark: I was wrong too. “I never imagined that the people in America with the most power would let companies get so close to things that one could lose control over without intervening.”
Tegmark: “The idea of corporate self-regulation is a joke in this case.” It “didn’t work out so well for the tobacco industry or for the pharma industry.”

Etzioni: I agree. Social media showed us how self-regulation goes: “This is the big tobacco moment for high tech.” “We don’t want to spend another 20 years to find out that AI companies didn’t exercise the appropriate level of self-discipline.”

Etzioni: A self-driving car will save your life, but “it doesn’t decide where to go. That’s a completely different system in the car than the thing that controls the brakes.” When I tell my car to head to Dunkin’ Donuts, the car doesn’t respond that it’s taking me to the gym instead because “it’s the second time you’ve gone to Dunkin’ Donuts this week.” We should box in other AI systems the same way.
Tegmark: “By default, machines should be given the least amount of access and power that they need to do their job.” “You don’t give every janitor in the Pentagon the nuclear codes.”
Etzioni: “We agree on off switches for AI. I’ve been advocating that since at least 2017 . We agree on labeling, on liability, on cyber standards, protecting kids.” The time to do that work is now.
Tegmark: “I agree with Oren: the time to actually act on this is now.”

Look back at these disagreements. Where Tegmark blames the machine, I blame a person. An engineer left a hole in the sandbox. A hacker typed the prompt. A politician found a new fear to run on. That’s why I’d box AI systems in rather than count on how they were raised.

Anthropic’s Amanda Askell compared getting Claude to behave to raising a child. But those of us with kids know how that goes. As I said in the debate, “the three-year-olds don’t listen to us, but the teenagers certainly don’t listen to us.”

articles.title: New Flyover Video Shows Latest West Seattle Link Design
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Sound Transit has officially reached the 30% design milestone on the West Seattle Link project, celebrating the occasion by releasing a new flyover video that shows renderings of the entire 3.9 mile planned light rail line between SoDo and Alaska Junction. Set to open by 2035 , the 3 Line is the next light rail project planned for construction in the wake of a feverish pace of grand openings over the past two years.

The new images, which reflect the project's design as of this past July, provide an illustration of the significant amount of value engineering that Sound Transit conducted on the line – work that likely saved the project from the chopping block this past spring as the agency grappled with a major budget gap.

From a slimmed-down SoDo station – which will be the northern terminus of the line until the Ballard Link project opens as early as 2042 (or as late as 2060) – to a more compact Alaska Junction, Sound Transit was able to drive down the cost of the line by more than $2 billion between 2024 and 2026.

That work to cut costs has come with real trade-offs for riders. The video shows the new plan for the 3 Line to enter a tunnel near Nucor Steel's West Seattle plant at SW Yancy Street, bypassing a planned station under Avalon Way SW that would have served a growing section of the neighborhood. Without that station, Sound Transit was able to redesign the location of the planned guideway and tunnel portal to avoid having to displace several high profile properties, including a portion of the West Seattle Health Club.

But in contrast with the infill station that opened in North Seattle late last month, it will not be possible to come back later and build Avalon Station down the road if Sound Transit's finances somehow turn around, or voters approve a Sound Transit 4.

On August 13, Sound Transit and the City of Seattle announced another major design refinement for West Seattle Link, one that would be hard to notice in a flyover rendering. A major transmission line that is currently located next to the dedicated busway through SoDo will be relocated closer to the planned light rail guideway, avoiding major disruptions on a nearby street.

"The new SODO segment design will relocate major City infrastructure, Seattle City Light’s 230 kilovolt and 26 kilovolt transmission poles and lines, entirely within the light rail project footprint in the SODO Busway," a City announcement noted at the time. "This means that Sound Transit will not need to move massive powerlines onto 6th Ave S, which significantly reduces construction and lasting impacts on adjacent properties and businesses. The new design is expected to save the project over $100 million and remove the risk of damage to other critical City transportation and water infrastructure."

Since the May 28 board vote that rebalanced the larger Sound Transit 3 (ST3) plan and kept West Seattle Link on track, Sound Transit officials have been touting how swiftly the agency has been moving and heading toward construction. In August, the board unlocked an additional $765 million in budget authorization, setting up a construction support services contract that includes preparations for the Duwamish River crossing.

Just last week, the board's system expansion committee approved another set of property acquisitions, including the West Seattle Corporate Center (the former Bartell Drugs corporate headquarters), which will become a major truck staging point for tunneling work to Alaska Junction. If approved by the full board later this month, that will mark the fifth set of property acquisition approvals that the agency has received, getting the agency's real estate team to work.

This week's flyover video makes work that is often happening behind the scenes more tangible for future riders, even if an opening date nine years in the future seems incredibly distant. Once the 3 Line is fully connected with the rest of the light rail network with the opening of Ballard Link, travelers getting from Westlake Station to Alaska Junction will see their travel times cut by 50%, a major upgrade from current C Line service. But there's a lot standing in the way of that benefit becoming reality.
For now, transit fans will have to live vicariously through YouTube.

articles.title: Dear Hendrix
articles.author: Eva Walker
paras: It’s the spooky season. And while I can’t wait to take you out trick-or-treating this Halloween, I wanted to preface the festive occasion with a little music for you (and all those folks reading this on their cell phones at home).

But when your mother is a professional DJ, a playlist can’t just be any old playlist. It has to include a little music education . So here goes! Musically speaking, when most people hear the word “goth,” bands like the Cure, Bauhaus, and Joy Division likely spring to mind. But goth, to me, is something different entirely.

I think of blues artists like Blind Willie Johnson, Son House, and Robert Johnson. These are songwriters and performers that taught me about darkness. They amplified American folklore, singing about figures like John Henry, the folk hero steel driver, the same way others might have heralded Hercules.

So I highlighted five songs by these artists who tell the story of the eerie, haunting American South, from its dark past to its chilling music. These artists, who thrived around the turn of the 20th century used their guitars like hammers, forging timeless masterpieces, despite the backdrop of slavery, the Civil War, lynchings, and extreme poverty. To me, they’re all goth.
P.S. There will be another letter going more into this interpretation of Goth through the lens of black history. But for now, enjoy the tunes.
“Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground” by Blind Willie Johnson (1927)

If the title isn’t goth enough for you already, wait until you give this song a listen. The track is all slide guitar and hums . What I love about these old recordings is feeling like I’m in the same room as the artist. The sound of the slide knocking against the fretboard and the sound of antique silence haunting in the background as Johnson hums is divine. The song displays great loneliness, grief, and heartache. Johnson lost his sight at a young age, when his stepmother threw lye in his face while arguing with his father. Later, in 1945, Johnson’s house was destroyed in a fire, but he stayed there living in the ruins until he died that September. If that isn’t the foundation for some dark music, I don’t know what is.

I’ve loved Son House for as long as I can remember. His song “Death Letter Blues” is goth at its finest. As soon as the track begins, we hear a slide screaming for answers. Son House sings with it, “I got a letter this morning, how do you reckon it read?” As the song continues, we learn the heartbreaking answer. The gal the singer loves is dead . The force behind Son House’s guitar is enough to make you want to get up and dance and holler, which is a strange feeling because he’s delivering to us some pretty awful news. Leave it to the blues to make death this vivacious … Son House is so dynamic, he makes his guitar sound like two people are playing at once—maybe it’s the angel and the devil on his shoulder—one on rhythm and one on lead. Everything sounds delightfully messy on the metal-bodied resonator. There is no wrong note Son House can hit in this song’s story of death and grief.
“Cross Road Blues” by Robert Johnson (1936)

Robert Johnson is likely the most influential blues guitarist to ever live. And his song “Cross Road Blues” is one of his most famous tracks—even now. Like the Son House song, this tune was recorded with just Johnson and his guitar. Although, also like the song above, the artist’s playing can easily be mistaken for two sets of hands. We don’t see the devil or the angel, we just hear them. After all, you can’t talk about Johnson without mentioning the infamous legend. How he went down to the crossroads in Clarksdale, Mississippi, and how he supposedly sold his soul to the devil in exchange for wicked guitar chops. Those chops have gone on to influence countless modern legends, from Keith Richards to Jimmy Page. It all begins on this song. (Fun fact: I played a show in Clarksdale in 2019 with my band, but the devil stood us up!)
“Last Kind Words Blues” by Geeshie Wiley (1930)

There is little known of the life of Geeshie Wiley. We aren’t even sure about her actual birth name (some say her real name may have been Lillie Mae). But while we don’t know much about her personal life, some of her music still lives on and, in many ways, that’s all the info we need. For example, just dive into this haunting track. It tells the story of her father going out to fight in the “German War” (World War I). The singer gives instructions on what to do with his body if he is killed. Geeshie’s haunting guitar, backed by the second guitar played by Elvie Thomas (aka L.V. Thomas), features a lead that mimics the main vocal melody. It establishes the mood, the feeling. It sounds like a cruel morning, cold and yet eerily stoic. You can almost know what it feels like to live in that moment thanks to this recording.
“Freight Train” by Elizabeth Cotten (1904)

We can’t talk about the blues without talking about Cotten-picking. The Venn Diagram of the two (the blues and the picking style) comes to us via the artist Elizabeth Cotten. Her song “Freight Train” is about death (my favorite subject!). It’s a common theme in the blues, but Cotten is no common songwriter or performer. She was left-handed and played a right-handed-stringed guitar upside down, plucking the song’s melody with her thumb and the bass line with her fingers. Her instrumentation was so good, it could easily be mistaken for a child’s lullaby. That is, if you didn’t listen to Cotten’s voice. Her shaky and aged voice told us all about loss and how it feels to her. Years later, Cotten was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for her foundational playing style—and rightfully so. Discovered by the Seeger family while working as a maid, Cotten won her first Grammy at 90 years old. Indeed, if you ever think it’s too late to start on guitar, Henny, just listen to Elizabeth Cotten. She can wake the dead.

Eva Walker is a writer, a KEXP DJ, one-half of the rock duo The Black Tones, and mom to her baby girl, Hendrix. She also co-wrote the book The Sound of Seattle: 101 Songs That Shaped a City , which was released in 2024. Every month for The Stranger , she writes a letter to Hendrix to share wisdom learned from her experiences—and her mistakes. Read all installments here.

articles.title: One Smart Cookie
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: “I’m actually in trouble with the City because of how honest I am on the socials,” Vince Vu deadpans, feigning concern. We’re seated around a tiny table in the front window of Anh Ơi Bake Shop at Sixth and Jackson, and the unvarnished candor I’ve come to know from his IG stories starts pouring out of him right from the jump. “They were like, ‘Actually, you know, as a Restored cohort member, it’d be really great if you could, like, run your ideas between us first?’”

He breaks character, grinning. “I was like, ‘No! What are you talking about? I’m not gonna do that. I don’t even say anything crazy online, guys.’ I’m just like, ‘Hey, it’s tough out here. Come in! Hello! I am selling sweet treats!’”

Behind the friendly face of this neighborhood baker is a skilled political strategy leader, community activist, and storyteller who knows how to light a fire and call folks to action. And after the sweet treats, that’s kind of the entire point of his shop.

Vu opened Anh Ơi Bake Shop in May 2026 as a place to sell his own Vietnamese-inspired cookies and cakes, as well as those of rotating guest bakers. The concept is a collaborative effort—he devotes a tall wooden shelf apiece to fellow Asian American bakers and their creations.

He snagged the 94-year-old storefront—in the historic former Osami’s Barber Shop space in Seattle’s Nihonmachi (Japantown)—as part of Seattle Restored, a program run through the Seattle Office of Economic Development, the Seattle Good Business Network, and Shunpike. The idea is to rent out and thereby revitalize previously empty retail spaces, then sublet them to new businesses rent-free for six months. He says he actually found the long-empty space himself, then worked with Seattle Restored to secure it via the Seattle Chinatown International District Preservation and Development Authority, aka SCIDpda. Seattle Restored’s participants also receive marketing help, enjoy professional photography of their wares, benefit from a citywide media campaign to help boost them up, and are connected with the property’s owners to negotiate a possible future lease. It’s a bullpen for entrepreneurs to try out their ideas, workshop their products, and tweak their business plans accordingly.

The timing seemed great: Anh Ơi would open just in time for the FIFA World Cup. “And we all know how that went,” Vu quips. Famously, the soccer-fan foot traffic that was promised by the city failed to materialize in the CID. That’s when Vu took matters into his own hands and started telling it like it is—via social media. In late June, he kicked off a reel by telling the camera, “I think the World Cup games in Seattle caused my business to have the worst sales day that it’s ever had.”

The FIFA crash and the viral-ish reel that followed were just the beginning of Anh Ơi’s online media blitz. Today, Vu is harnessing as much marketing reach as the socials can bring him, mostly via reels. These include his takes on popular memes with CID themes inserted, and installments of “The Anh Ơi School of Business,” where he “explain[s] business lessons I learned because I was forced to.” Other times, he’s just telling us that persimmons are in season and to look out for all the delicious pastries about to happen.

Another quirk of the project: Everything in the store is prepackaged. “Yeah, my production isn’t here,” he explains. “I bake my own stuff in SoDo, and I buy the wrapped pastries from the other vendors and then sell them here. I’m just shelves. I’m a grocery store.”

The treats themselves are as fascinating as his business model. Gaze at each shelf in Anh Ơi and read all the different placards with the bios of the bakers and the photos of their faces, and it’s like they’re baking little diary entries for us. On the day I interviewed Vu, baker Cindy Vuong, who operates as Sweet Dream Bakes, had pineapple bun cookies and lotus mooncakes filled with salted egg yolks on her shelf, while Alison Shiu from PãoBāo Bread was selling Portuguese-Chinese snacks like corn focaccia buns dressed with dried shrimp chili oil and sesame cookies loaded with spicy Huang Fei Hong peanuts. (To my chagrin, her char siu chouriço bao had sold out—that’s Portuguese chouriço sausage and char siu, aka Chinese barbecue pork baked inside a crispy-crusted milk bread bun.) La Chinita’s Cocina melds Mexican and Muslim Southeast Asian flavors—among owner Philicia Saephan’s goodies is an ube-s’more brownie topped with beef-gelatin-based halal marshmallows. And Vu himself makes a strawberry corn milk cookie and a fried banana cookie that both go crazy and sell out consistently. These shelves are essentially a personal to-do list for me.

There’s a self-serve cooler case in back for things like durian ice cream and canned cà phê sữa đá. The shop also has room for a coffee/tea cart, where several different pop-uppers—like Muni Cafe, whose menu includes, for example, a matcha latte crowned with a cloud of banana cold foam—have camped out for six-week stints.

When asked how he curates his gallery of bakers, Vu says he began with people he’d met in the farmers market circuit. “I’d popped up at lots of different events, festivals, markets… and you quickly figure out who the competitive vendors are and who the chill ones are, who are very collaborative, very open. When I opened this shop, I called all the chill ones and was like, ‘Hey, I love your stuff. Let’s sell together.’”

Vu also recruits new bakers at farmers markets and other pop-ups, plus he gets new folks coming in with samples all the time. He says he always chats with prospective bakers and makers at length to see if they have matched energy, especially since he enjoys hearing people’s food stories. “What I really love is when someone’s like, ‘Oh, I made this because it reminds me of my mom,’ and I can be like, ‘Oh wow, really? Why? Tell me about your mom.’”

Whatever’s happening inside Anh Ơi on any given day, it’s always hyper-creative, and it’s always about to change. If you eat something you love, you can always check the shelf’s sign and follow the maker online to see where else they sell their stuff. In fact, that’s the whole idea: to be a marketing engine for the superhero pantheon of indie Asian American bakers.

How did Vu cook up such a clever concept? “I’ve been a baker my entire life,” he replies, “like as a subplot. I have a master’s in public policy, and I worked in politics—I worked for Dow [Constantine, former King County Executive]. That’s what brought me to Seattle. And then I worked in tech, and even then, I was baking on the side.

“But when I left tech,” he says, “and you hear this all the time, but tech left me completely spiritually defunct. I felt like I was doing evil. Like, ‘I’m an evildoer. I’m not making the world better.’ And that really bothered me.” He decided to do something not evil for a living instead and took a four-month sabbatical to Vietnam to figure out what that was. “I knew I wanted to do something tactile, with my hands. And I wanted to do something that’s very unapologetically me, which is something Asian American– and community-focused. So I sort of marinated in those ideas.”

From the trip emerged the idea for Anh Ơi. The name is Vietnamese for “hey, you,” specifically when addressing an older male. Per the shop’s website, “it’s a tender little call to someone you care about—a brother, a lover, a friend. It’s playful, it’s warm, it’s how we pull each other close.”

The shop’s concept was nudged along into reality by Vu’s background in government, and his years of tech and marketing experience have proved useful too. “I knew that government policies make it really hard to start any business,” he said, “and especially a food business. So I was like, ‘Let me do it in a way that gets around a lot of that stuff.’” Vu says that, by and large, people don’t know—and the city doesn’t make it easy for them to know—that they can start a food business in such a creative, nonstandard way. He suspects he’s gotten some superfluous attention from county health inspectors for publicly telling folks how it’s done. “It’s so funny,” he says, “because the city has sent so many inspectors here, and like, I worked for the government for 10 years. So like, try me, right? Please try me.

“I always tell people if I ever ran for office,” he says, “I’d be a single-issue politician, and that issue would be: We have to fix our small food business process. Like, people are getting crazy diarrhea from shredded lettuce and finding glass in their frozen bread, or whatever is happening from the big conglomerations. And yet you’re gonna come here over and over to try to pick on my tiny-ass business that hasn’t broken any rules?”

As of press time, Vu’s Seattle Restored tenancy expires October 15. What happens next isn’t totally up to him. “I really want to stay. It depends on Restored—I need their blessing.” Hopefully, he says, once he gets it, he’ll be able to coordinate with SCIDpda and the building’s owners directly going forward.

Vu isn’t shy about his jingoism when it comes to the CID, its rich history, and its scads of very beautiful buildings. When he was applying for the Seattle Restored program, the neighborhood was nonnegotiable for him: “This business makes no sense anywhere but the CID.” As such, he’s frustrated with the city’s lack of investment in the neighborhood. He points to a recent application filed by McDonald’s for the prominent former Bartell Drugs space at Fourth and Jackson. “I’m like, ‘Do you want that to happen to the CID?’ So, I tell my friends, ‘There’s a lot of space available here. The spaces are rough. But we can make them better! We’ll invest in the neighborhood—that’s what we do.’”

It’s a tenuous situation, Vu says, to simultaneously rescue a historic district from both empty storefronts and evil empires. “Honestly, the city should be throwing money at us. There’s great food here. We talk about it like it’s one of the gems of the city. These old buildings are great. Tourists come here—it’s one of their main stops. But the city won’t invest in it, and no one is moving here. Why not? The city could be helping us.”

The challenges of operating a business in the CID aside, Vu’s project sure seems like a success on paper. “I’m the most successful Restored installation they’ve had,” he admits. “I do really well here. But from a revenue perspective, it’s still incredibly difficult… I think the bigger thing I’m trying to highlight is that, hey, I’ve had all these supports, and I have a ton of community help, and I get money from these people. And still, even then, whew. It is rough out here.”

With Seattle rent, permit fees, and other operating costs sharply rising to more comedic and nonsensical heights every year, this city deeply needs more creative, unconventional business-building—especially the food kind. Something needs to change, as soon as possible.

To put a bow on it, Vu concludes: “Let’s challenge what the local food landscape looks like. Right? It doesn’t have to be just solitary genius jerk chefs out here. It can be small people you’ve never heard of, sharing ideas and helping each other make them real. That’s why I do what I do.”
