paras: The leaves are finally starting to fall and there is no better place to admire King County’s incredible scenery than from a historic Metro bus. The annual Metro Employees Historic Vehicle Association (MEHVA) Fall Foliage Tour is back this year on October 25. Ride on one of the historic buses in MEHVA’s fleet through the Cascade foothills. Buses depart from 6th Ave S & S Royal Brougham Way (one block from Stadium station) at 11am and will return around 3pm. Tickets cost $10 and the group will stop for lunch along the way.

If you prefer to stay in Seattle, the Washington Park Arboretum is incredible this time of year. The arboretum is located just west of Madison Park, near stops for routes 8, 11, 43, 48, and the G Line. UW station is the closest Link station, about a 20 minute walk from the park.

articles.title: Tug-of-War Over New Transportation Funding Heats Up in Bellevue
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Bellevue City Council is on the cusp of approving a pair of new funding sources to bolster transportation infrastructure later this fall, but the fight over what exactly those new dollars should fund is far from settled. The debate playing out now is set to decide which transportation projects the Eastside's largest city prioritizes over the next decade, as it prepares to accommodate significant housing growth around public transit.

This week city officials formally presented a set of scenarios that outlined how Bellevue would use projected revenue from a potential 0.1% increase in the city's sales tax rate as well as a $20 car tab fee, unlocked from a transportation benefit district that the city has been considering tapping into since 2023. The sales tax bump would be expected to generate around $100 million for transportation infrastructure over 10 years, with the car tab only bringing in $20 million over the same period.

Sustainable transportation advocates in Bellevue have been pushing for a major infusion of resources to help reduce deaths and serious injuries, and that push has been backed up by a bloc of councilmembers standing behind the idea of prioritizing safety investments. But many of Bellevue's business interests are pushing for more investments in "underperforming" intersections to make it easier to drive around the city.

If the Council decides to adopt both the sales tax hike and the car tab next month, Bellevue would be poised to invest an additional $35 million over a decade in bike and pedestrian improvement projects, as well as $16.4 million more in neighborhood traffic calming. Combined, those two categories would amount to 41% of the city's total transportation spending, roughly aligning with levels proposed by Bellevue Transportation Director Andrew Singelakis during an initial budget discussion this spring.

The "major projects" category would amount to a full 35% of spending and 33% of new dollars, with the majority of that new spending devoted to completing the next phase of Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) through the BelRed neighborhood. Framed as a multimodal project, the $74.8 million connection would create an alternative for pedestrian-hostile Bel-Red Road – which the Council decided against making safer for people on bikes in 2024 . But with two general purpose lanes beefing up the need for property acquisition, the benefits of the project for people who walk and bike in Bellevue won't really align with its cost.
There's also the fact that the road cuts right through what is intended to be a new park for the future residents of BelRed.

The scenarios laid out on Tuesday do invest plenty in vehicle capacity in their own right. Scenario two, which includes only the sales tax increase, includes $18.9 million in new funding for projects specifically intended to address driver travel times on top of $49.3 million under the status quo. That includes $10 million to widen two intersections to improve traffic flow. With scenario three, which includes the new car tab fee, that would increase to $25 million, getting another intersection widening across the finish line.

There's also the issue of the Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to build a pedestrian bridge over I-405 between Downtown and Wilburton and create a brand new multimodal connection as well as an opportunity for placemaking. Under either scenario 2 or 3, the $265 million project would receive a $10 million investment, freeing up dollars that had been set to go to the crossing from the general fund – dollars that could potentially go to any other city spending. Recently the City of Bellevue received buy-in from several regional governments to tap into tax-increment financing to pay for a much bigger share of that project's total cost.

These potential funding sources recently won over a major Bellevue stakeholder. Three years ago, the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce had initially opposed the idea of tapping into the unutilized transportation benefit district, which cities like Seattle have long been using to fund infrastructure. But now they've come around, officially conveying support for the move Tuesday night. But the business group, which has convened a Bellevue Mobility Coalition to weigh in on transportation issues, has conditions.

The group has framed an intense desire to see the sales tax revenue generated by the 0.1% increase – "paid largely by businesses" – serve the city's high-growth areas like Downtown, Wilburton, Factoria, and Eastgate. The smaller tranche of car tab funding, the group said in an October 6 letter, should "primarily benefit neighborhoods."

In comments Tuesday night, a Chamber representative also told councilmembers they want to see any additional funding that comes in beyond projections get devoted to vehicle infrastructure – namely intersections that are considered "deficient" in terms of how much delay drivers experience getting through them. The group also made clear that they don't support the idea of repurposing traffic lanes to create bicycle facilities, one of the most cost-effective ways for cities to make streets safer.

"Our support depends on four things. First, funding for Spring Boulevard Zone 3, 120th Avenue NE Stage 4, and the Grand Connection stays sufficient to complete the projects," Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, told councilmembers. "Second, the underperforming intersections fund is increased and focused on growth corridor arterials with the first $10 million of any surplus sales tax collections dedicated. Third, vehicular capacity is not reduced for bicycle facilities except as a last resort. Fourth, sales tax revenue is not shifted to neighborhood programs that the car tab should fund."

Mariya Frost, Vice President of Government Affairs for Kemper Development Company (a member of the Bellevue Mobility Coalition), went even further than the Chamber, requesting that the Council put the revenue sources to a public vote and suggesting the proposals invest too much in walking and biking. The company, which recently announced an intention to sell its holdings in Bellevue, has been actively involved in transportation decisions in the city going back decades.

"If council decides to move forward without a public vote, project funding must prioritize traffic congestion relief and accommodating vehicular travel associated with Bellevue's growth," Frost said. "The rationale I've heard is that we need to balance the system across all modes, but it makes little sense to disproportionately pour millions of dollars into lower demand infrastructure while the roadway network carrying nearly 70% of our workers and residents is actively breaking down."
But so far Councilmember Jared Nieuwenhuis has been the lone voice on council framing either scenario as investing too much in walking and biking.

"Throughout the different scenarios, there's substantially more funding for bikes and pedestrians than vehicles," Nieuwenhuis said. "You're looking for that balanced approach, [a] multimodal approach. I totally agree with that, but I'm also cognizant of the fact the vast majority of people that who come into our city do so in a vehicle, in their car."

Other councilmembers have only expressed frustration that the investments the city has planned aren't able to be implemented sooner, but also haven't signaled a willingness to rebalance any of the funding scenarios by prioritizing safety projects over intersection widenings.

"Every year at this time, we have the Walk and Roll to School Day commitment proclamation. And I always think to myself, is it really safe to expect that our families are going to ask their kids to walk or roll to school?," Councilmember Lynne Robinson said. "And I know every year it gets a little safer, but we have so many holes in our infrastructure that most families I don't think do feel comfortable having their kids get to school independently, and that just creates a huge line of cars and congestion in our neighborhoods."
Councilmember Naren Briar made similar remarks, echoing comments she made back in April about wanting to see more funding devoted to neighborhood traffic calming and safety upgrades.

"If a seven-year-old has no sidewalks or a crosswalk to rely on when waiting for the bus in the dark at 7am, those children are our top concern for me, and their safety and their well-being, as opposed to prioritizing one mode over the other," Briar said. "I think neighborhood improvement is what I would really like to see. I understand that if we get to a place where taxes have to be raised, I do firmly believe that it needs to prevail through the scenario that benefits the neighborhoods the most."

While the attempt to strike a "balanced approach" illustrates Bellevue's current state as formerly car-oriented suburb trying to find a path toward being a more cosmopolitan place, there are signs that the reality of trying to keep planning around cars is starting to sink in.

"As we grow over the next 20 years, there will be limited capacity for additional vehicle facilities," Deputy Transportation Director Mark Poch said. "Right of way is limited. We have really good regional transportation we need to connect to, a lot of people connect to that by foot or by bike, as you know. Trying to find that balance so that we're able to meet that growth is really the key objective and making sure that we were aligned with what the community thinks – not one for one, but in the same ballpark, I think was important."
Bellevue's budget deliberations are set to continue throughout this month, with major decisions coming at November 3 and 10 meetings ahead of a final vote on November 17.
This story has been corrected to clarify the percentage of total spending set to go to pedestrian & bicycle and neighborhood traffic calming.

articles.title: Shelf Life
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: As he leads me on a tour of Scarecrow Video, longtime buyer Mark Steiner spots former employee Xoe Amer in the new releases section and waves. Steiner, who started working at Scarecrow in 1992 and retired in September, has worked with Amer’s mom, witnessed Xoe grow up, and seen her work at Scarecrow’s erstwhile coffee stand VHSpresso.

“Just seeing Xoe browsing the shelves, that’s second-generation right there. Right behind the counter, too,” he says, gesturing toward Sophia Soriano, an employee whose mother, Rebecca Soriano, cofounded Scarecrow in 1988. “It blows my mind. We’ve endured, no matter what got thrown at us, and it boggles my mind that we’re still here.”

This kind of relationship is emblematic of Steiner’s 34-year stint at Scarecrow, which has surpassed the entirety of Blockbuster’s 29-year corporate retail era in the US; international stores closed in 2020. He has seen the store go from around 1,000 titles to over 156,000, and nearly every single one has passed through his hands. Even he still sometimes gets overwhelmed by Scarecrow’s massive inventory. “Every day I do my job, and I leave and I have 50 things to watch,” he says. “So I always tell people, ‘I get intimidated in this place too, and I’ve been here.’” As he points out, nobody will live long enough to see every movie in the store.

Steiner may well be the longest-tenured video store employee in history, but you wouldn’t know it from his affable, modest demeanor. “I just put my head down and came to work,” he says. “And the other corollary that is equally important is that it’s a really cool place to work, and everybody who’s run it has always been nothing but supportive.” In 2006, a tree fell on his house, nearly killing both of his children, and Scarecrow bolstered him through the crisis. They also allowed him to work four days a week, enabling him to spend more time raising his kids.

Steiner lights up when he talks about film, gesticulating and reciting a steady stream of trivia from the annals of his cinematic knowledge. As a child in Detroit, he learned to read by poring over film critic Leonard Maltin’s annual movie guide. While home sick with chickenpox one day, he was wowed by North by Northwest on TV. The summer he turned 10, he rode his bike to the theater to see Star Wars , which he says “blew up my world.” His family got a VCR when he was 11, and each of them got to pick out a movie. Steiner chose Robert Altman’s M*A*S*H because he liked the TV series, which was based on the film, and watched it daily. Altman eventually became his favorite director, and some 40 years later, he’d let M*A*S*H actor Tom Skerritt into Scarecrow and chat with him.

At 13, his bubbe took him to see Raging Bull , his first R-rated movie. “That was the first movie that really knocked my socks off that I saw in the theater,” he remembers. Around the same time, his cousin, who worked at a record store in Detroit, introduced him to artists like Mott the Hoople, Lou Reed, and David Bowie, sparking a lifelong love of music and “rabid” record collecting habit. “I’m an omnivore, I guess,” he says. “I like what I like, but I always want more.”

At Michigan State University, Steiner and a friend launched a film club, screening mostly foreign films on campus. He also frequented the Lansing video store Video to Go, which stocked a wide variety of titles and which he calls an “early model” for Scarecrow. After graduation, he moved to Seattle, having absorbed romantic visions of the Pacific Northwest from the films McCabe & Mrs. Miller and Trouble in Mind and the Tom Robbins novel Jitterbug Perfume . There, he became a regular at Scarecrow Video’s original Latona Avenue location. One day in 1992, he walked in feeling completely burned out from working in social services, and the staff encouraged him to apply for a job. Although he accidentally missed a meeting on his first day, the team embraced him warmly, and thus began a decades-long career. The following year, Scarecrow moved to its current Roosevelt location, and the buyer position was created for Steiner.

Steiner’s life is inextricable from his vocation. Even his 1998 wedding vows came from the 1945 romantic drama The Clock , directed by one of his favorite directors, Vincente Minnelli. In the film, Judy Garland (who would later marry Minnelli) and Robert Walker play a young couple who wed within the course of a 24-hour whirlwind romance. Similarly, Steiner and his now-wife fell in love during a 24-hour first date, so the lines felt apt. “We were like, okay, good enough for Judy Garland and Vincente Minnelli,” he says.

His curiosity and humility have served him well, helping him discover titles beyond his own taste. He credits his kids with broadening his horizons and stresses the importance of “know[ing] you’re a dumbass.” “You gotta pay attention, you gotta hear from people, because if it was just me, it’d be all Westerns on the main floor,” he says. “With any curating, I think you can view it with your knowledge, but that shouldn’t be the beginning or the end.”

From his office on the second floor, Steiner could overhear customers talking to staff, which helped him gauge demand and learn about films he wouldn’t have otherwise. No day as a buyer was exactly the same as another. The position demanded grit, adaptability, persistence, and an ability to build relationships with distributors. “It’s a mix of listening to people and just being really, really diligent and detail-oriented, and that’s sometimes a slog,” Steiner says.

Scarecrow almost went out of business in 2014 due to competition from streaming services; Steiner helped them survive as they became a nonprofit and introduced their popular DVD-by-mail program across the country in 2021. “He’s been a stabilizing force through all of that stuff. He’s paid his dues, he’s earned some rest,” veteran employee Joel Fisher says.

Fisher, who helped spearhead Scarecrow’s transition into a nonprofit, is taking over as buyer. He says that the connections Steiner has cultivated with distributors will be the most difficult thing to replace. “That’s going to be a thing that I just have to earn through time and build from scratch. I’ll probably do things in my way and just try to figure out a good way to move forward,” Fisher says. “Things are always changing in this realm. We’re actually in a really good place now that the pendulum has swung back towards people understanding the importance of physical media.”

Fisher will miss Steiner’s dedication. “Mark’s been around forever, so he remembers everything that happens, and he’s really passionate about helping people out,” he says. “He’s dealt with all the special orders and availability checks, so he’ll go out of his way if people are searching for a thing. If he can find it, then he’ll leave no stone unturned, and he’s always really good with that.” Once, Steiner tracked down a VHS copy of Apocalypse Now for an older woman who wanted to watch it because it was her late husband’s favorite film—at the time, DVDs could not be easily paused with the intent of resuming later in the same spot, and she couldn’t sit through a three-hour movie. The year Napoleon Dynamite came out, Steiner went to Costco to buy up their stock because of the extreme demand for it around Christmas, and it was so popular that people were begging to buy copies in the Scarecrow parking lot when he returned.

Steiner has a gold mine of stories about brushes with celebrities and film industry behemoths. He’s seen stars like Bridget Fonda, Roger Ebert, Alejandro Jodorowsky, and Quentin Tarantino (a former video store employee himself) walk through Scarecrow’s doors. When legendary director Bertrand Tavernier came to SIFF in 1997 to promote his film Capitaine Conan , Steiner invited him to the store and followed him around for three hours as he rifled through titles and remarked on them in a thick French accent. He once sat in on director Werner Herzog, actor Crispin Glover, and former Scarecrow employee Norm Hill recording the commentary for Herzog’s film Even Dwarfs Started Small , in which Herzog uttered the sage wisdom, “Chickens are something that frighten me because they are so stupid… When you really take a close look into the eyes of a chicken, it’s really, really weird.”

Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love used to patronize the Latona location. Once, late Scarecrow cofounder George Latsios, who would read back customers’ first and last names in order to memorize them, loudly repeated “Kurt Cobain” several times, having never heard of the Nirvana frontman. “He was trying to keep a low profile, and George is like, ‘Hello, Kurt Cobain! Oh, you’re Kurt Cobain,’ and you see these people in the store, their ears perking up,” Steiner recalls. Still oblivious, Latsios inquired what Cobain did for a living and asked, “You aren’t one of those grunge musicians, are you?” When Cobain responded that he was, Latsios earnestly wished him luck. (For context, this was a week after Nirvana appeared on Saturday Night Live .)

As for Love, she favored British dramas like Brideshead Revisited due to her time living in the UK and would rent a “shitload of tapes” at a time, until Love and Cobain’s nannies inevitably returned them late. She incurred so many late fees that her accountant had to have a talk with her, according to Rebecca Soriano, but Steiner calls it a “wonderfully symbiotic relationship,” since her fines helped support the store.

He’s invigorated by the new wave of younger generations’ enthusiasm for film. “We’re really engaging more and more with customers, and that’s what I’m most excited about,” he says. “It used to be this boys’ club.” He’s seen a rise in interest in body horror, such as Coralie Fargeat’s The Substance , David Cronenberg’s films, and Louise Weard’s Castration Movie series, which sold a staggering 30 copies.

It’s important to Steiner that Scarecrow persists as an archive. He says many people don’t realize that they don’t sell off anything from their stock, unless they’re upgrading existing titles. “If you came in here as a kid and saw something, it should still be here for you 30 years later,” he says. Of Scarecrow’s 100 rarest titles, 88 aren’t even in the Library of Congress.

In retirement, Steiner looks forward to spending time with his wife and his dog Gracie and continuing to pursue his twin passions of movies and music. He’s excited about the possibility of working with Rebecca, who is retiring from teaching third grade, to bring film education to classrooms. Since 2019, he’s also hosted a radio show called Soundtrack Cinema from 7–8 p.m. each Thursday on SPACE 101.1 FM. “I’ve just always wanted to share cool things, and radio is perfect for that,” he says. Every week, he creates a themed soundtrack, using film and TV scores, needle drops, and other film-related music.

Nevertheless, he’ll still be found roaming the shelves of Scarecrow from time to time. “I mean, how could I not?” he says. “I’ve had this at my fingertips for my whole adult life, so I couldn’t conceive of not taking something home when I come in.”

articles.title: Pollet and Dreher Hone Their Pitch to Urbanists in LD46 Race
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Depending how the November election goes, the residents of the 46th Legislative District in Northwest Seattle could have a new state representative after Rep. Gerry Pollet drew a relatively strong challenge from former federal prosecutor Will Dreher. Dreher has staked his campaign on a bid to lead the charge for artificial intelligence regulations, while Pollet is leaning on his experience, and his campaign has pitched him as the real progressive in the race.
In a three-way race, Pollet finished the primary on top, with 51.6% of the primary vote. Dreher won nearly 31% and has serious ground to close if he hopes to pull off the upset.

Plus, the dynamic of the race got a little weird after the primary. Tech entrepreneur and progressive rabblerouser Ron Davis, who The Urbanist Election Committee (on which I serve) endorsed , was eliminated after pulling in 16% of the vote. Rather than endorsing the other challenger or simply riding off into the sunset, Davis enthusiastically endorsed Pollet , and took to sharply attacking Dreher and defending Pollet via two long posts on his website, Rondevous .

Also catching criticism from Davis was The Stranger , which endorsed Dreher in the primary. "Let’s unleash this blue-blooded Yankee on the billionaire tech lobby that writes our laws in Olympia," The Stranger wrote. That endorsement likely sealed Davis' loss, although the gulf between the candidates was large enough he may have lost anyway.

"I came back to the same inexorable conclusion I reached in early July: that The Stranger's endorsements really are that powerful, and that it's nearly impossible for a progressive to overcome its influence even with a strong campaign and a lot of grassroots support," Davis wrote in August.

After his primary loss, Davis alleged Pollet – despite his earlier decision to challenge him for his seat – wasn't so bad, and was actually a standout on a number of issues, including education and progressive taxation.

The move came as a surprise to some urbanists who tracked Pollet's anti-urbanist positions early in his career, such as opposing bike lanes in Wedgwood and obstructing statewide housing reform. In contrast, Dreher is a regular cyclist and has pledged to be a reliable pro-housing vote.

"I bike commuted for about four or five years after the pandemic started downtown from my house in Ravenna, and you know one of the things that I very quickly learned as a bike commuter was, I mean, for me personally at least, that I was not comfortable biking with traffic," Dreher told The Urbanist . "And that the number one thing for both safety and to increase the actual uptake of biking seems to have obviously not just protected bike lanes, but protected bike trails and making sure that we have a robust connected trail network."

Dreher said the state should invest more in transit and pursue congestion pricing to make roads work better for all, following in the footsteps of New York City's new highly successful congestion pricing system in Lower Manhattan.

"Manhattan is a very small island in the grand scheme of things relative to the population of New York City," Dreher said. "Downtown Seattle is a land constrained area, with only so many ways to get in or out, and congestion pricing - it's true - is useful for and can be used for raising revenue, but you know I view its primary purpose as modifying behavior in a way that helps the fight against climate change, right? And in a way that helps make our downtown both less congested, have less local pollution, and in general be helping to encourage folks to use alternative ways to get downtown."
While he granted it would take time, Dreher expressed interest in being part of a coalition advancing congestion pricing.

"The good thing is that we now have some cities that are actually exploring, and not just exploring in theory, but actually in practice using congestion pricing, and the sky has not fallen," Dreher said. "My hope would be that we can start to build a coalition around what I think is a fairly sensible policy solution that more cities in the United States should be using. [...] It's something that I think makes a ton of sense. It's something that I think we just need to start having that conversation now in order to make it become a reality at some point in the near future."

On housing issues, Dreher told The Urbanist he is interested in pursuing a statewide funded inclusionary zoning program and in exploring a land value tax. He also pledged to be a reliable vote on housing abundance, although his campaign website did formerly use some "neighborhood character"-type language that Davis portrayed as dog whistles for "not in my backyard" (NIMBY) housing opponents. Dreher has since removed the language and told The Urbanist that it was an honest mistake, rather than a dog whistle.

Dreher's linguistic choices aside, Pollet was such an obstacle as chair of the House Local Government Committee that I named him to the "zeroes" list in our annual legislative recap after the 2021 and 2022 sessions.
Davis himself noted the cost of delays from housing reform holdouts like Pollet when in his campaign rollout interview with The Urbanist back in March.

“Those years were low-interest-rate years. We could have tens of thousands, maybe 50,000 or 100,000 more modestly-priced homes in the region right now, and they would be bidding over us, instead of us bidding over what’s left. And that’s a really huge and ugly, frustrating dynamic,” Davis told The Urbanist at the time.

That frustration seemed to extend to members of the Democratic caucus, who removed Pollet as chair following the 2022 session. Democrats came back in 2023 and finally succeeded in passing statewide middle housing reform via House Bill 1110. That law recently bore fruit as the mandate kicked in last year in many cities, including Seattle , which finally phased out restrictive single family zoning and allowed fourplexes or greater citywide after more than a decade of flirting with the idea to no avail.

Pollet ended up voting for HB 1110, but not before pressing his colleagues to pass an amendment allowing up to a quarter of an affected city's residential land to be carved out of rezones by citing displacement risk. In practice, the logistics of the displacement-risk carveouts have proven complicated enough that most cities have avoided them.

Fast forward to 2026 and Pollet has the endorsement of some of the legislature's most well-known urbanists, like Rep. Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne), and Nicole Macri and Shaun Scott (D-43rd LD, Capitol Hill).

"I know I've evolved," Pollet told The Urbanist during an interview last month. "It's important to evolve and learn and realize that I wasn't as steeped in it as I needed to be on some aspects of middle housing, I was much more focused on housing issues relating to multifamily and transit-oriented development than middle housing."

Pollet portrayed himself as better at spotting when local activists were simply making excuses, rather than raising genuine concerns, such as the frequent excuse that neighborhoods need more robust infrastructure before they can accept housing growth, whether beefier roads or utilities or bigger schools.

"One of the things I learned is that listening to people who said, 'Well, we don't have the infrastructure,' was a NIMBY response that we needed to say, 'We're going to force you to have the infrastructure if you truly don't.' But we're not just going to take your word for it because it's often a NIMBY response, and that's an example of where I feel I was very conscious of my changing position that we have to force local governments to do that."

In illustrating how he's evolved and become an asset for the urbanist coalition that rattled off a string of policy wins in recent legislative sessions, Pollet pointed out he helped ensure that statewide parking reform passed in 2025 .

"I not only voted for it, but when it came to the floor of the House, we were briefed on it in caucus, and it ran into a roadblock that nearly pulled it from the schedule," Pollet said, before launching into a story about he helped broker an agreement between his colleagues and disability rights advocates to ensure those concerns did not derail the parking reform bill.

Davis, who met with The Urbanist along with Pollet last month shortly after endorsing him, vouched for his former rival, saying he was a big help in passing parking reform, which Davis was lobbying for on behalf of the Sightline Institute. (Of course, not so helpful overall that he opted against challenging him for his seat.)

Given his background, Pollet is naturally sympathetic to environmental concerns and is skeptical of efforts to streamline the State Environmental Policy Act, which has been criticized as a needless hurdle for housing projects, often hijacked by degrowth activists and NIMBYs to delay projects. Pollet's roots and his road to politics are in environmental law.

"I went to law school at the UW to be an environmental public interest attorney," Pollet told The Urbanist during a September interview. "[I] led the effort to stop Hanford from being a high-level nuclear waste dump, working with the Yakima [Tribe] to protect Gable Mountain, which is sacred to them, and ran the statewide ballot initiative to stop that in 1986, and then founded the organization leading work on the cleanup of Hanford, and along the way, you know, I was very active on many of our groundbreaking environmental laws in the state, including helping draft the Growth Management Act. I was one of the five or six authors of our state Superfund law model, and lobbied on many many environmental laws and helped pass many of them in our state."
Dreher, like Davis, is a Harvard Law trained attorney. Dreher followed in the footsteps of his father, who was a top environmental lawyer for the Clinton and Obama administrations.

Dreher famously clerked for Brett Kavanaugh , the Trump-nominated judge who won a lifetime appointment on the U.S. Supreme Court in 2018. Dreher signed a letter of support for that bid, along with fellow former law clerks. Davis used that as a frequent attack line on the campaign trail, but it didn't seem to fully resonate with voters, given the primary result.

After Kavanaugh's Supreme Court nomination happened in 2018 and the sexual assault allegations against him came out, Dreher said he changed his mind and withdrew his support. Dreher later that year signed onto a second letter supporting an FBI investigation of the allegations.

In 2019, Dreher joined the Department of Justice under the Trump administration as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Western District of Washington. His website notes "Dreher has the rare distinction of having prosecuted 25 January 6th insurrectionists." He spent over five years as a federal prosecutor, before leaving to join private practice as a litigator at the firm Keller Rohrback.

Dreher helped lead the firm's artificial intelligence litigation group and was appointed Co-Lead Interim Class Counsel in the copyright infringement class action Hendrix et al. v. Apple, Inc . The case alleges copyright infringement over texts Apple fed into its large language model or LLM, without permission from the authors or publishers.
Dreher has made reining in AI platforms and the tech giants behind them as a centerpiece of his campaign.

"The primary impetus for me getting in this particular race now was really just how rapidly accelerating, I think, our challenges with artificial intelligence and technology more broadly," Dreher said. "So like data privacy, mass surveillance, social media use with kids. There were just a number of tech issues that I've been working on in my current job for the last couple of years, but that I just had seen very little progress on at the state legislature, and I think even beyond that, very little focus on those issues."

Dreher pointed out that the Trump administration seemed to be going in the opposite direction, embracing a rapid expansion of AI applications for short-term financial gain. The state, meanwhile, has been flatfooted when it comes to regulating AI, in his estimation.

"My daughter, who's nine, always talks about how she wants to be a teacher when she grows up," Dreher said. "And Melania Trump in March, came out and had a rollout with a robot teacher and said, 'This will be the future of education.' And I'd say that was really the moment where it fully clicked or crystallized – that I just felt like I needed to do something to try to make sure that that was not the future of education, and more broadly, to try to kickstart or jumpstart our state to start taking seriously that battle."

On the other hand, Dreher's critics – with Davis at the vanguard – have questioned whether Dreher is ready to take on the tech giants so heavily invested in infusing AI into American life. They've pointed out that employees at the AI firm Anthropic were a top source of donations for Dreher's campaign, much of that money from out of state. Pollet, himself, seemed to take offense that Dreher was seeking to claim ownership of education reform, AI, and data privacy regulation issues, which he saw the state legislature as already making significant headway on.

"My thought is same thing goes as education. How would he know? He's not lobbied one day on these issues in Olympia," Pollet told The Urbanist . "There are legislators who know a lot more than him about those issues, and like part of that is the data center issues, right? And you know, he started this campaign, and I don't think he knew that I and others, working with [Rep.] Beth Doglio, had introduced what is viewed nationally as a model bill in terms of regulating data centers. And on data privacy, I don't think he knows, for example, what the battle has been in this state, and we have really strong champions on data privacy."
While not as versed in urbanist bread-and-butter topics as Davis, Dreher still sees himself as the standard-bearer for those issues now that Davis has been knocked out of the race.

"I frankly appreciate Ron's expertise and experience on a number of the issues that we've talked about, housing and transit issues in particular," Dreher said. "I was happy that that was one of the focuses in the race, and I intend to continue to make it a focus for the rest of the race. But now... the voters maybe have a somewhat simplified decision to make between myself and Representative Pollet."

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
In July 2026, we updated this map to include tapas bar Ocho, choose-your-own-beefy-adventure steakhouse Asadero Prime, and neighborhood Thai mainstay Pestle Rock.
